setup: The SPRAT application is opened in a browser for a requirements workshop involving privacy and security stakeholders.
action: A team member starts creating and linking web-system requirements, privacy policies, and security policies within the workbench.
expected_observation: The workspace supports collaborative capture and linking of requirements to privacy and security policies, reflecting SPRAT as a workbench for aligning web-system requirements with policy concerns.

setup: A project is at the requirements and analysis stage, with design decisions not yet finalized, and the team is also preparing for review and compliance validation.
action: An analyst opens SPRAT to document early requirements, then later revisits the same analysis to assess a proposed change and check policy compliance.
expected_observation: SPRAT remains usable throughout early requirements work, review, change impact analysis, and compliance checking, without requiring design to be finalized first.

setup: A user account exists for each role: administrator, project manager, analyst, and guest.
action: Each role signs in and opens the same project workspace.
expected_observation: The system grants access according to role, showing administrative controls to administrators, project coordination functions to project managers, analysis functions to analysts, and limited read-only or restricted access to guests.

setup: A project workspace is open and the user has permission to add project content.
action: The user creates new entries for a goal, a scenario, a policy, a requirement, and a legal-compliance note.
expected_observation: Each item is saved and visible in the workspace as a distinct captured artifact, with its content preserved for later reference and linking.

setup: A project contains an existing goal, policy, scenario, requirement, and a draft analysis note.
action: The user links the requirement to the goal, the goal to the policy, and the analysis note to the relevant scenario.
expected_observation: The linked items appear connected in the workspace so that the rationale chain between goals, policies, requirements, scenarios, and derived analyses can be followed from one item to another.

setup: A requirement exists in the project with at least one recorded policy or legal-rule link.
action: The user opens the requirement's trace view and selects the option to trace it back to its origin.
expected_observation: The system displays the source policy or legal rule associated with the requirement, allowing the user to follow the trace backward from the requirement to its originating rule.

setup: A goal or requirement is already linked to a policy reference in the workspace.
action: The user opens the trace details for that goal or requirement.
expected_observation: The trace record shows the source policy reference, the exact policy passage or clause used to justify the item, and a short rationale explaining the connection.

setup: A project contains multiple goals, requirements, and policy sources with established trace links.
action: The user opens the traceability report for a selected goal or requirement.
expected_observation: The report clearly shows which requirement supports which goal and identifies the policy or legal source that justified the goal or requirement.

setup: A goal is linked to more than one requirement, and one requirement is also linked to more than one goal and policy.
action: The user views the relationship map for the selected items.
expected_observation: The workspace displays the multiple links in both directions, showing a many-to-many relationship among requirements, goals, and policies instead of collapsing them into a single connection.

setup: Two requirements share the same policy source and contribute to the same higher-level goal through different trace paths.
action: The user opens the traceability visualization for the goal.
expected_observation: The system reveals the shared policy dependency and overlapping paths explicitly, making the common links visible rather than hiding them behind one chosen route.

setup: A requirement belongs to multiple trace paths, and the team has designated one of those links as the primary link.
action: The user opens the requirement's trace view.
expected_observation: All relevant links are shown, and the designated primary link is clearly marked as primary while the other links remain visible as alternate paths.

setup: Two analysis versions exist for the same project, prepared by the same or different analysts.
action: The user selects both analyses and starts a side-by-side comparison.
expected_observation: The system displays the two analyses next to each other so the user can compare their content without switching between separate screens.

setup: Two analyses have been selected for comparison and contain partially overlapping goals, policies, and requirements.
action: The user runs the comparison view.
expected_observation: The comparison highlights items that match in both analyses, items that differ, and items that appear in only one analysis.

setup: Two analysts have independently traced the same requirement within separate analysis versions, but each linked it to a different source policy.
action: The user compares the two analyses for that requirement.
expected_observation: The comparison makes the conflicting source-policy traces visible, showing that the same requirement was justified by different policies in the two analyses.

setup: Two analysts have separately built analyses for the same project, each with their own recorded decisions and trace links.
action: A reviewer opens both analyses and compares them after the independent work is complete.
expected_observation: The system allows comparison of the independently built analyses while preserving each analysis's reasoning, trace links, and decision history for review.

setup: A project manager is signed in to SPRAT and opens an analysis project that already contains reviewed items, analyst comments, comparison outputs, and established traceability links.
action: The project manager opens the review panel, adds a comment to an analysis item, runs a compare-analysis view between two published analyses, and opens the traceability-check view for a selected requirement.
expected_observation: SPRAT displays the review, comment, compare-analysis, and traceability-check functions for the project manager, and the newly added comment and traceability-check results are shown within the project context.

setup: A guest account is signed in and the project contains approved materials, along with published analyses that may or may not be comparison-enabled by the project settings.
action: The guest opens an approved material from the public view and attempts to access the compare view for two published analyses.
expected_observation: The guest can view the approved material; if compare access is enabled for the project, the published analyses can also be compared, otherwise the compare option is hidden or blocked with a read-only access message.

setup: An analyst is signed in to SPRAT and opens a workspace containing analysis items that can be organized into different classifications such as policy area, risk theme, and source type.
action: The analyst assigns classifications to several analysis items using the classification management controls and later switches the current view filter to a different classification scheme.
expected_observation: The analysis items remain organized under the selected classifications, and the same items can be browsed through different classification views without losing their organization data.

setup: An artifact is already stored in SPRAT and is known to belong naturally to more than one view, such as both a policy obligation view and a supporting evidence view.
action: The analyst assigns a second classification to the same artifact while keeping the first classification unchanged.
expected_observation: The artifact appears in both relevant classifications, and each classification view shows the artifact without removing or replacing the other classification.

setup: An analyst is reviewing an analysis item that currently has an initial placeholder classification, and the item history tracking is enabled for the project.
action: The analyst reclassifies the item to a more accurate category after refining the analysis.
expected_observation: SPRAT updates the current classification while preserving the previous classification in the item history, so the reclassification can be reviewed later as part of the audit trail.

setup: A traceability link exists from a derived analysis item to a source item, and the source item is later revised or marked inactive in the project.
action: The analyst opens the derived item and views its traceability details after the source item status has changed.
expected_observation: The derived-from link remains visible in the trace view, and the system still shows the relationship to the original source item even though the source is revised or inactive.

setup: A trace chain has been created across multiple generations of analysis items, with a clear direct parent and one or more upstream ancestors.
action: The analyst opens the traceability chain for the final item in the sequence.
expected_observation: SPRAT displays the full multi-level derived-from chain, preserves the historical ancestry where relevant, and clearly identifies the direct parent of the current item.

setup: A requirement trace includes a direct policy link plus one or more intermediate goals or policy versions that explain how the requirement justification evolved over time.
action: The analyst opens the traceability record for the requirement and inspects the justification path.
expected_observation: The direct policy link is shown most prominently, while intermediate goals or policy versions remain preserved in the trace so the justification path can be understood.

setup: An existing body of analysis work is prepared for import from a legacy repository, and the migration process for SPRAT has been initiated for that dataset.
action: The project manager starts the migration of the legacy analysis work into SPRAT.
expected_observation: SPRAT begins importing the legacy work in a controlled migration flow rather than requiring a full manual rebuild, and the migrated content becomes available in the target workspace.

setup: Legacy analysis work has been migrated into SPRAT, including source references, comments, and trace links that were present in the original repository.
action: A reviewer opens the migrated work and inspects the traceability and supporting context for several items.
expected_observation: The migrated work retains its traceability and contextual information well enough for review, so reviewers can follow the relationships and trust the provenance of the imported analysis.

setup: A migration package contains active analysis content, linked source references, and additional legacy formatting artifacts and historical clutter from the original system.
action: The migration is executed for the package.
expected_observation: SPRAT brings over the core active content and the links needed for current work, while unnecessary formatting artifacts or historical clutter are not imported when they are not needed.

setup: A migration queue includes active projects, authoritative source documents, and supporting items required to preserve current traceability for ongoing work.
action: The migration is run with prioritization for current work.
expected_observation: SPRAT migrates the active projects, authoritative source documents, and traceability-critical items first, making the current work available before lower-priority legacy content.

setup: An active trace link in SPRAT points to a policy source and is supported by an obligation reference, current notes, and evidence attachments needed to justify the trace.
action: A reviewer opens the trace link details for the active item.
expected_observation: The trace detail view includes the linked policy source, the specific obligation reference, and the current supporting notes or evidence needed to explain or prove the trace relationship.

setup: A project manager account has review-only permissions, and a guest account has read-only permissions, both with access to the same project area.
action: The project manager and the guest each open the project views available to their roles.
expected_observation: The project manager can use review-only capabilities without edit privileges, and the guest can access only read-only views without any ability to modify content.

setup: A guest is signed in to SPRAT and attempts to access a project that includes both public and restricted information, with editing disabled for guest accounts.
action: The guest tries to edit an analysis item and opens a restricted detail view.
expected_observation: SPRAT blocks the change attempt and prevents access to restricted details, while keeping the guest limited to permitted read-only content.

setup: A guest user is viewing a project workspace that contains sensitive notes, draft legal-compliance content, and trace links. The project owner has not granted the guest any explicit access rights.
action: The guest opens the sensitive notes area and attempts to view a draft compliance note and its associated trace links.
expected_observation: The system blocks access to the sensitive note, hides the draft legal-compliance information and unapproved trace links, and displays an access-denied message indicating that project-owner approval is required.

setup: The user is on an office desktop or a remote work laptop with a supported web browser, and the organization has enabled web access for the project.
action: The user signs in through the web interface from the office network or from a remote location.
expected_observation: The project workspace loads successfully in the browser and the user can access the analysis tool through the web without requiring a separate desktop application.

setup: A sensitive project is configured with network and device restrictions, and the user is attempting remote access from outside the approved corporate network.
action: The user signs in from a remote device to open the sensitive project, using stronger authentication as prompted, and attempts access without explicit approval for the especially sensitive workspace.
expected_observation: The system allows access only if the device or network is approved and the stronger authentication succeeds; for the especially sensitive project, access remains blocked until explicit approval is granted, with a clear denial shown when approval is missing.

setup: A sensitive project is under active review, and an analyst needs urgent temporary access outside the normal approval path.
action: The analyst submits an urgent access exception request for the sensitive project and provides the stated reason for the exception.
expected_observation: The system grants access only for the approved exception window, records the exception in the audit log with requester, reason, approver, and expiry time, and automatically revokes the access when the time limit expires.

setup: A new analyst opens a fresh project workspace with the default capture and trace tools enabled and minimal onboarding guidance available.
action: The analyst enters a simple requirement note and creates a basic trace link using the provided capture workflow.
expected_observation: The system lets the analyst complete the capture and trace task with short, clear prompts and minimal required steps, while presenting the new item and its link in the workspace.

setup: A low-risk project is being edited by a new analyst who has already completed the basic workflow tutorial and is working with ordinary source documents.
action: The analyst edits a trace item, reclassifies it to an allowed ordinary category, and links it to a standard source type.
expected_observation: The system permits the edit, reclassification, and linking without forcing heavy approval or review steps, and the updated trace is saved successfully.

setup: A sensitive project contains a trace item created by a new analyst, and the project is configured to require review before publication.
action: The new analyst attempts to finalize or publish the trace without obtaining review from a project manager or experienced analyst.
expected_observation: The system prevents publication, shows that review is required, and keeps the trace in a pending state until an eligible reviewer approves it.

setup: A very sensitive project or a project with a complex policy set is being set up by a new analyst, and guided onboarding is enabled.
action: The analyst starts the setup flow and selects or enters classifications for the project content.
expected_observation: The system provides guided setup instructions, example acceptable classifications, and routes the configuration to a short administrator or project manager review before the setup is accepted.

setup: The analyst is reviewing a comparison view that explains how two items differ or match.
action: The analyst opens the inline help or explanation adjacent to the comparison results.
expected_observation: The system displays a clear explanation of how the comparison was interpreted, including what was considered a match, mismatch, or partial match.

setup: The analyst is creating or editing an analysis item in the workspace.
action: The analyst enters a title or name and writes a descriptive summary for the item, then saves it.
expected_observation: The system stores and displays both the title or name and the description for the analysis item.

setup: The analyst is documenting a scenario in the analysis tool.
action: The analyst records who performs the action, what event triggers it, and what result follows.
expected_observation: The scenario form captures the actor, trigger, and outcome as distinct fields and shows them in the saved scenario record.

setup: A requirement is being marked as originating from a policy source.
action: The analyst tries to save the requirement without adding any trace links to the supporting policy source.
expected_observation: The system rejects the save or flags the item as incomplete and indicates that trace links are required before a policy-derived requirement can be accepted.

setup: A trace item contains missing classification data or conflicting classifications across related fields.
action: The analyst saves the item with the incomplete or inconsistent classifications.
expected_observation: The system flags the missing or inconsistent classifications clearly and does not silently accept the item as valid.

setup: The analyst runs a structural consistency check on an analysis containing links, classifications, and several related requirements.
action: The analyst requests validation of the analysis structure.
expected_observation: The system reports whether required links are present, whether classifications are used correctly, and whether obvious trace gaps exist, highlighting structural issues for review.

setup: The analyst opens an analysis item containing content that may be questionable but requires human interpretation.
action: The analyst runs the content check or validation review on the item.
expected_observation: The system clearly flags the questionable content for attention without making the semantic decision itself, leaving the final judgment to the analyst or reviewer.

setup: An analyst is logged into the Security and Privacy Requirements Analysis Tool and is viewing an existing traceable item such as a policy, requirement, or scenario.
action: The analyst adds a new trace link from that item to another artifact.
expected_observation: The trace is saved with the analyst's identity and a timestamp showing when the trace was created, and both details are visible in the trace record or audit view.

setup: A goal exists that can be justified by more than one policy, and a requirement or scenario is available that explains an indirect relationship to the goal.
action: The analyst links several policies to the goal and creates a trace from the goal through the intermediary requirement or scenario instead of directly to the source policy.
expected_observation: The goal shows all supported policies, and the indirect trace is accepted and displayed as explainable through the requirement or scenario rather than being rejected as incomplete.

setup: A requirement has been derived from another requirement or from a scenario, and the source item already exists in the repository.
action: The source requirement or scenario is edited, renamed, or otherwise updated by an analyst.
expected_observation: The derived requirement still displays its derived-from link to the original source item, and the link remains visible even after the source item changes.

setup: A requirement has been derived from another requirement, and the derivation chain includes more than one upstream item.
action: The analyst opens the derived requirement and inspects its lineage information.
expected_observation: The system shows the immediate parent in the derived-from chain, making the direct origin of the requirement clear and unambiguous.

setup: An existing artifact such as a goal, requirement, policy, or trace is editable and the audit trail feature is enabled.
action: An analyst modifies the artifact's content or relationship and saves the change.
expected_observation: The audit trail records what was changed, who made the change, and when the change occurred, and the entry is available for review.

setup: A goal, requirement, policy, or trace has at least one previous saved version in the system.
action: An analyst opens the artifact's history or version record after a change has been made.
expected_observation: The system preserves the prior version or sufficient reconstruction detail so the earlier state can be viewed or recovered from the history.

setup: A requirement or policy has been edited after other items were derived from it or reviewed against it.
action: The analyst opens the changed artifact and requests the impact or downstream trace view.
expected_observation: The system shows which downstream items were derived from the changed artifact or were reviewed against it, allowing the analyst to see affected items.

setup: The repository contains artifacts ready for export and the user has access to the export function.
action: The user requests an export in a machine-readable format such as CSV or JSON and then requests an export in a human-readable format such as PDF or Word.
expected_observation: The system produces at least one structured export file and one human-readable document export, both successfully generated for download or sharing.

setup: An artifact includes trace links and audit metadata such as author, timestamps, and change history.
action: The user exports the artifact to a supported export format.
expected_observation: The exported file retains the trace links and audit metadata, allowing the relationships and history to be reviewed outside the application.

setup: A user without an authorized export role is signed in and can view export options in the interface.
action: The user attempts to perform a raw export of project data.
expected_observation: The system denies the raw export request and indicates that the user's role is not permitted to access raw exports.

setup: An analyst is preparing information for external sharing and an unfiltered export of the same data exists in the system.
action: The analyst attempts to release the unfiltered export to an external recipient.
expected_observation: The system requires a redacted or approved version for external sharing and blocks or rejects the unfiltered export.

setup: The export content includes sensitive information such as personal data, legal interpretations, unresolved disputes, or security weaknesses, and the system has sensitivity-based export controls enabled.
action: The user requests an export containing that sensitive content.
expected_observation: The system either redacts the sensitive portions or blocks the export according to the sensitivity of the content, and the user is informed of the restriction.

setup: An export is identified by the system as potentially revealing an individual's identity or exposing a control gap, and the export is otherwise eligible for sharing.
action: The user tries to release the export without obtaining approval first.
expected_observation: The system withholds release until explicit approval is recorded, and the export remains pending or blocked until approval is granted.

setup: A lower-role user, such as a reviewer or viewer, is signed in and the export contains draft comments, sensitive source links, and personal data.
action: The user generates an export of the project content.
expected_observation: The exported output is automatically reduced in detail by excluding draft comments, sensitive source links, and personal data.

setup: A user is signed in with limited clearance or access scoped to a different project, and the target export contains information above that clearance or outside that project scope.
action: The user attempts to export the restricted information.
expected_observation: The system blocks the export and clearly indicates that the requested information is above the user's clearance level or outside their authorized project scope.

setup: A change request has been submitted for a requirement whose ownership is unclear because multiple teams claim responsibility and no authoritative owner is assigned in the project registry.
action: A reviewer opens the change request and attempts to approve it without an assigned authority confirmation.
expected_observation: The request is marked as pending review, a clear ownership-unclear flag is shown, and the system does not allow approval until a user with confirmed authority explicitly approves or assigns ownership.

setup: The designated responsible person for a pending analysis item is marked unavailable for the current review window, and a fallback approver has been configured for the project.
action: A new ownership-sensitive change is submitted for review while the primary responsible person remains unavailable.
expected_observation: The system routes the item to the configured fallback approver, displays the fallback relationship explicitly, and records an auditable trail showing why the fallback was used and who handled the review.

setup: A classification rule and a permission policy already exist with prior approved versions, and historical decisions are retained in the system.
action: An administrator updates the classification and permission settings for the project.
expected_observation: The original decision records remain unchanged, a new version is created with provenance information, and the history view shows the prior and current versions rather than overwriting the earlier decisions.

setup: A classification, rule, or permission has been modified in a project that already has downstream analyses relying on the previous values.
action: A reviewer opens the change details after the update has been saved.
expected_observation: The system shows what changed, the timestamp of the change, and a list of impacted analyses or reports, with the affected items clearly identified in the change summary.

setup: An analyst is preparing a review package for a security-sensitive requirement, and the system has validation checks enabled for consistency and completeness.
action: The analyst submits a review containing a broken trace link, a missing justification, or another mistake that would weaken confidence in the analysis.
expected_observation: The submission is blocked or returned for correction, the specific validation issue is highlighted, and the system prevents the flawed review from being treated as authoritative until the mistake is resolved.

setup: A requirement has been traced to a source policy through one or more intermediate goals, and the policy has at least one prior version retained for justification history.
action: A user opens the requirement's traceability view.
expected_observation: The visible trace link shows the source policy, preserves the intermediate goals or policy versions used to justify the trace, and allows the reviewer to follow the justification path without losing context.

setup: A requirement has been associated with several business goals, and one policy has already been linked to multiple requirements in the traceability model.
action: An analyst opens the traceability graph for the requirement and the policy.
expected_observation: The system displays all of the requirement's linked goals and all requirements driven by the same policy, confirming that many-to-many trace relationships are preserved and visible.

setup: A requirement was derived from another requirement and then further elaborated into a scenario during analysis.
action: A reviewer opens the derived requirement's lineage view.
expected_observation: The system shows the upstream requirement and scenario that produced it, making the derivation connection visible rather than presenting the item as standalone.

setup: The same policy statement appears in two separate analysis routes leading to the same requirement.
action: A user inspects both analysis routes from the requirement trace view.
expected_observation: The policy statement is retained in both paths or is shown once with references to both routes, and no trace information is lost or suppressed because it appears in multiple analyses.

setup: An item belongs to more than one trace path, including a direct policy path and an indirect goal-based path.
action: A reviewer opens the item's dependency or provenance view.
expected_observation: The system displays all relevant links for every applicable path, allowing the reviewer to see both the direct and indirect trace relationships together.

setup: A project is classified as sensitive, and a guest account plus an analyst account not assigned to that project both have login access to the platform.
action: The guest or unassigned analyst attempts to open the sensitive project's requirements and traceability screens.
expected_observation: Access is denied or restricted according to the tighter project controls, and the user is prevented from viewing project content they are not assigned to.

setup: A sensitive project has administrator-defined location or device restrictions enabled by policy.
action: A user attempts to access the project from a disallowed device or location.
expected_observation: The system enforces the configured restriction, blocks access, and indicates that the rule is driven by the project's sensitivity and administrator policy.

setup: A requirement has been mapped to multiple goals, and one policy has been linked to several requirements in the current project.
action: A user views the requirements-to-goals and policy-to-requirements relationship summary.
expected_observation: The system shows all mapped goals for the requirement and all requirements driven by the policy, reflecting the one-to-many and many-to-one relationships without collapsing them into a single link.

setup: A classification is currently referenced by active trace links, access rules, and compliance reports that depend on its current value.
action: An administrator attempts to change that classification in a way that would break those links or reporting outputs.
expected_observation: The system locks or protects the classification from direct change and presents a message explaining that the edit would break trace links, access rules, or compliance reporting.

setup: A classification change has been proposed that would alter traceability, access, or compliance evidence, and the proposed change is not merely an obvious typo correction that preserves meaning and visibility.
action: A user submits the classification update.
expected_observation: The system routes the change through review before it can take effect, and only trivial corrections that do not change meaning or visibility are allowed to bypass review.

setup: A reviewer is signed in with permission to edit a record in the Security and Privacy Requirements Analysis Tool, and an analysis item on screen contains an obviously misspelled or mistyped value that can be corrected immediately.
action: The reviewer applies the correction directly in the record and saves the change.
expected_observation: The updated value is shown on screen, and the audit trail records the original value, the corrected value, the timestamp, and the identity of the person who made the change.

setup: The first release version of the tool is deployed for a pilot workspace with standard users, analysts, reviewers, and project managers configured.
action: A user opens the application and navigates through collaboration features, traceability views, and access-controlled content.
expected_observation: Core collaboration functions are available, trace links and change history can be viewed, and role-based access control restricts actions according to the user's assigned role.

setup: The first release is being configured for a new customer without any pilot-customer exception or unresolved compliance obligation requiring additional capability.
action: A product administrator reviews the available feature set for release planning and attempts to enable deep workflow automation, advanced analytics dashboards, and broad repository integrations.
expected_observation: Those advanced capabilities are not included in the first release by default, and the system or release configuration indicates they remain out of scope unless explicitly justified as essential for a pilot customer or compliance need.

setup: A pilot customer has documented that one deferred capability is essential to satisfy a specific compliance obligation, and the team is working within the normal capture, trace, and compare workflow.
action: An analyst activates the smallest available version of that capability to complete only the required compliance task.
expected_observation: The minimal capability operates only within the existing capture, trace, and compare flow, preserves access control and redaction, and still allows the analysis to be reviewed and revised without broader feature expansion.

setup: A pilot exception or compliance workaround has been identified for a sensitive project, and ownership roles are assigned within the project team.
action: The team records the exception workaround and assigns accountability for it.
expected_observation: The workaround is owned by the person accountable for the pilot or compliance outcome, typically the project manager or lead analyst, and the ownership is visible in the record.

setup: A workaround is needed to bridge a gap in the current release, and SPRAT is being used as the system of record.
action: A project lead logs the workaround in SPRAT and enters its supporting details.
expected_observation: The workaround is stored as a time-bounded exception with a reason, the workaround method used, and either a target date or a closure condition.

setup: A workaround has been recorded in SPRAT with a deadline, an integration dependency, and a compliance acceptance condition.
action: One of the stopping conditions occurs, such as the deadline being reached, the required integration becoming available, or the compliance evidence being formally accepted and archived.
expected_observation: The workaround is marked as ended or closed, and it no longer applies to subsequent work in the affected process.

setup: A requested feature is being evaluated for a pilot customer or compliance need, and the team is assessing whether it is truly required under the normal SPRAT workflow.
action: The evaluator confirms that the need cannot be satisfied without the feature and that there is a real deadline or contractual expectation.
expected_observation: The feature is classified as essential only when both conditions are met; otherwise it is not treated as essential.

setup: A feature has already been approved as essential for a specific pilot or compliance outcome.
action: The team configures the feature for use in the project.
expected_observation: The feature remains limited to the smallest direct path for the approved outcome and does not expand to broader teams, extra document types, or wider reporting.

setup: A user is performing a routine, low-risk action that matches an approved template or a previously validated pattern.
action: The user takes the fast path to complete the action.
expected_observation: The action is allowed with reduced steps, while the record still captures who performed it, what changed, when it happened, and the source policy or requirement that justified it.

setup: A user is working on a request that changes a sensitive classification, legal compliance status, access permission, or creates a new trace link.
action: The user attempts to use a fast path that skips additional review steps.
expected_observation: The system blocks the shortcut and requires the extra steps before the change can be completed.

setup: A sensitive project has access restrictions enabled, approved corporate networks are defined, trusted devices are registered, and remote access requires stronger authentication and explicit approval for especially sensitive work.
action: A user attempts to access the project from an unapproved location or device, or from a remote location without the required stronger authentication or approval.
expected_observation: Access is denied unless the user is on an approved corporate network or trusted device and meets the stronger authentication and approval requirements for the level of sensitivity.

setup: An urgent-access exception is required for a sensitive project due to an exceptional business need.
action: A manager approves and activates the urgent-access exception for the user.
expected_observation: The exception is recorded in the audit trail, the access is granted only for the approved limited duration, and the time limit is clearly visible for later review.

setup: The tool is monitored across normal working hours on a typical business day, with availability tracking enabled.
action: Users attempt to access the system during scheduled working hours.
expected_observation: The system is reachable during normal working hours and remains continuously available or near-continuously available with no significant interruption to user access.

setup: A user has an in-progress analysis open with unsaved edits, and a brief service interruption occurs.
action: The system goes down momentarily and then becomes available again.
expected_observation: The user's current work is preserved, no entered content is lost, and the user can resume from the previous state quickly after recovery.

setup: An analyst is signed in to the web application on a standard office laptop with a project open that contains existing analyses, trace links, and a large imported evidence set.
action: The analyst searches for a control by keyword, opens a trace link from the results, saves an edited analysis, loads a dense analysis record, compares two output views, imports a large evidence file, and applies a bulk status update to multiple items.
expected_observation: Each operation completes within a normal interactive workflow without the interface freezing, timing out, or preventing the analyst from continuing to work.

setup: An analyst is using the application during a normal day-to-day review session with a project containing several hundred traceable items and previously saved analyses.
action: The analyst performs a typical search, navigates between trace links, and saves a small analysis edit.
expected_observation: The application may show brief processing feedback, but search, trace navigation, and saving remain clearly usable and do not feel noticeably sluggish in a way that interrupts routine work.

setup: A project is open and approximately thirty to forty users are actively working in the system at the same time, including analysts searching, tracing, and saving analyses.
action: One analyst performs a standard search and opens several trace links while other users continue their concurrent activity.
expected_observation: The analyst can complete the workflow with acceptable responsiveness, and the system remains usable for the group without widespread delays or session instability.

setup: The system is under a burst workload caused by a heavy collaborative review session, a large import in progress, multiple bulk updates, and several cross-project comparisons being initiated at the same time.
action: A reviewer continues searching, tracing, and saving analyses while the burst workload is active.
expected_observation: The system remains available and responsive enough for meaningful work, with any slowdown staying within acceptable bounds and without blocking the ongoing collaborative activity.

setup: A user has access to a normal office or remote working environment with a modern web browser, standard keyboard and mouse, and no special client software or browser extensions installed.
action: The user opens the application in the browser, signs in, and performs a typical capture or trace task.
expected_observation: The application works end-to-end through the web interface without requiring special tooling, desktop add-ons, or a nonstandard environment.

setup: A new analyst account has been created and assigned access to a training or starter project containing a simple capture and trace workflow.
action: The analyst follows the on-screen workflow to create a basic capture item and add a trace link without receiving live expert assistance.
expected_observation: The analyst can complete the basic capture and trace tasks with only minimal guidance from the interface, such as prompts, labels, or inline field hints.

setup: A newly onboarded analyst has access to both basic capture/trace functions and advanced classification and comparison functions in a training environment.
action: The analyst attempts to use the advanced classification and comparison features after completing basic capture and trace tasks.
expected_observation: The advanced features require more explanation, reference material, or guided instruction than the basic tasks, and are not presented as equally self-explanatory.

setup: A project is marked as very sensitive or uses a complex policy set that includes nuanced classification rules and comparison interpretation guidance.
action: The user opens the project setup or classification workflow for that sensitive project.
expected_observation: The system provides guided setup steps, example acceptable classifications, and inline explanations that help the user interpret comparisons correctly.

setup: An existing analysis record has been migrated into the system and later changed through a review or update process, with original notes, timestamps, or source references available in the historical record.
action: A user opens the migrated analysis and then views the changed version after the update.
expected_observation: The original context remains visible or recoverable as part of the record history, rather than being overwritten by the newer version.

setup: A project contains trace-linked analysis items with audit trail entries such as who changed what, when, and from which source, and the project is prepared for migration or export.
action: An administrator migrates the analysis data to another workspace or exports it for external review.
expected_observation: The exported or migrated output retains audit trail details and traceability relationships so that the history of the analysis can still be followed after transfer.

setup: Two analyses are available for comparison, and they come from different projects with clearly different policy contexts and unrelated subject matter.
action: A reviewer attempts to compare the two unrelated analyses side by side.
expected_observation: The system warns that the analyses are from unrelated contexts or prevents the comparison from being treated as meaningful, rather than presenting it as a valid policy comparison.

setup: A low-risk project is being used in a self-service workflow by a trained analyst, and the analyst is not in a senior approval role.
action: The analyst creates a basic capture item and then attempts to change official compliance wording or submit a final approval action.
expected_observation: The basic capture task remains self-service, but the final approval or official wording change is blocked pending a senior role or delegated approver.

setup: A low-risk project includes a source item that is sensitive in nature, such as a legal interpretation note or a policy exception record.
action: A standard analyst attempts to capture or update that sensitive source item without initiating any review workflow.
expected_observation: The system requires a review step before the sensitive source can be finalized, even though the broader project is low risk.

setup: An analyst is viewing a classification record that contains a clear labeling mistake, such as an incorrect typo-level sensitivity tag that does not affect meaning or visibility.
action: The analyst changes the classification immediately to the obvious correct value.
expected_observation: The system allows the immediate correction without forcing a review, because the change is clearly a non-substantive correction.

setup: A user is preparing to change the classification of an item, but the effect on traceability, access permissions, or compliance evidence is unclear from the available context.
action: The user submits the classification change while uncertainty remains about its downstream impact.
expected_observation: The system treats the change as review required and does not apply it immediately until the potential impact has been assessed.

setup: The project backlog contains a minimal compliance-focused capability that is explicitly intended only for the current pilot or regulatory need, and a proposed change request is raised to expand it to support additional teams, more document types, broader reporting, or future-proofing features.
action: A product owner attempts to approve the expanded scope for inclusion in the current release plan.
expected_observation: The scope review marks the expansion as out of bounds for the stated requirement, and the release plan retains only the original minimal essential capability without the added teams, document types, reporting, or future-proofing work.

setup: The access policy configuration for office and remote web access is not yet finalized, and the project is waiting for the security policy decision that defines whether access is allowed, denied, or requires additional controls in each context.
action: A request is made to document or enforce web access rules for both office and remote locations without first supplying the project-specific security policy.
expected_observation: The system or requirements review does not apply a fixed access decision, and the unresolved access conditions remain flagged as dependent on the final security policy rather than being assumed or automatically enabled.

setup: The capacity planning assumption for the tool has only been informally estimated at 'a few dozen' concurrent users, with no validated performance target beyond that range.
action: A stakeholder asks for an approved concurrency limit higher than the tentative estimate, or requests acceptance criteria for loads above a few dozen simultaneous users.
expected_observation: The capacity requirement remains unresolved and is not promoted as a validated performance commitment beyond the tentative 'a few dozen' user assumption.
